clinicalPearls: A rare malignancy arising within the ectopic thyroid tissue of a thyroglossal duct cyst, usually discovered incidentally after excision of a presumed benign midline neck cyst
Presents as a painless midline neck swelling that classically moves upward with tongue protrusion and swallowing, indistinguishable clinically from a benign cyst
The great majority are papillary carcinomas, reflecting their origin from displaced thyroid follicular tissue along the tract of thyroid descent
Diagnosis is usually histological after Sistrunk excision, since preoperative aspiration rarely identifies the malignancy within an inflamed cyst
When cancer is confirmed, evaluation of the orthotopic thyroid gland is important, as synchronous papillary carcinoma may be present
Management combines the Sistrunk operation with individualised consideration of thyroidectomy, radioactive iodine, and TSH suppression depending on risk features
Prognosis is generally very good, mirroring the favourable behaviour of well-differentiated papillary thyroid carcinoma
reference.pathophysiology: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a remnant of the embryological tract along which the thyroid descends from the foramen caecum of the tongue to its cervical position, and it may retain ectopic thyroid follicular tissue. Malignant transformation of this tissue, most often into papillary carcinoma, gives rise to thyroglossal duct carcinoma. Because the epithelium is of thyroid follicular type, the tumour behaves like a well-differentiated thyroid cancer and can, in a minority of cases, coexist with a primary carcinoma in the orthotopic gland, raising the question of whether disease is truly primary within the cyst or represents metastatic spread.
additionalDifferentials: Dermoid or epidermoid cyst of the midline neck
Enlarged delphian or pretracheal lymph node
Papillary carcinoma of the orthotopic thyroid with nodal spread
Midline branchial or other developmental neck cyst
additionalInvestigations: Neck ultrasound to characterise the midline cyst and assess the thyroid gland and lymph nodes
Assessment of the orthotopic thyroid for a synchronous primary carcinoma
Histological examination of the Sistrunk excision specimen for definitive diagnosis
Serum TSH and thyroid function to confirm euthyroid status
Serum thyroglobulin as a post-treatment marker when thyroidectomy is performed
Cross-sectional imaging if invasive or nodal disease is suspected
redFlags: Rapid enlargement, fixation, or irregularity of a previously stable midline cyst
Associated cervical lymphadenopathy suggesting nodal spread
A synchronous suspicious nodule in the orthotopic thyroid gland
Invasion of adjacent structures on imaging
reference.prognosis: Outcome is generally excellent given the predominantly papillary, well-differentiated histology, with adverse features being invasive disease, nodal or distant spread, and a coexisting higher-risk primary thyroid cancer.
pitfalls: Assuming every midline neck cyst is benign and omitting careful histological examination of the excised specimen
Failing to assess the orthotopic thyroid for a synchronous carcinoma once cyst malignancy is found
Relying on preoperative aspiration, which frequently fails to detect malignancy in an inflamed cyst
Performing simple cystectomy rather than the Sistrunk procedure, risking incomplete excision and recurrence
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: The Sistrunk operation, excising the cyst, the whole tract and the central portion of the hyoid, is the primary surgical treatment
Evaluate the orthotopic thyroid gland and consider total thyroidectomy where a synchronous primary carcinoma or high-risk features are present
Give radioactive iodine ablation after thyroidectomy for higher-risk differentiated disease
Provide TSH-suppressive levothyroxine therapy in appropriate risk categories
Assess cervical lymph nodes and undertake neck dissection where nodal disease is confirmed
Follow up with serum thyroglobulin and neck ultrasound for recurrence
Manage within a multidisciplinary endocrine surgery and oncology team
